reader.title: "An Episode of Border Life" (lynching of a gambler called Jim)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: The sketch narrates fifteen or twenty miners breaking into the jail, taking the accused gambler and hanging him until dead (A1).

As narrated, a 'committee' of fifteen or twenty miners seized a prisoner from guards and hanged him for murdering a police officer, telling him he had 'got to swing for it' (A1); the account is a single undated, unplaced reminiscence, so the verdict applies to the story as told.
Only one reprinted feature sketch, credited to the Pittsburgh Post and giving no date, town, state or full name, describes the episode (A1).

summary.text: "An Episode of Border Life" is a first-person sketch, credited to the Pittsburgh Post and reprinted in the Somerset Press of Ohio on 16 June 1881, describing the lynching of a gambler called Jim by miners in an unnamed Western mining town.
In the story, fifteen or twenty men left a coroner's inquest, broke into the jail and hanged the gambler for shooting a police officer, then posed for a photograph with the body.
The sketch gives no date, place, surname or race, and no other report of the episode appears in the coverage.
The narrator, called Ramsey, was woken early one morning by a companion who told him to hurry or he would "miss the lynching."
At Jim Beggs' gambling saloon a coroner's jury had been impaneled over the body of a police officer, laid out on two faro tables with a coiled rope and hangman's noose on top of it.

According to the first sworn witness, two gamblers had quarreled over bets the previous evening, and when the officer told them to stop the noise, one of them drew a gun and shot him through the heart.
Before the witness finished, a large man in a red flannel shirt took up the rope, said "Boys, that's enough: come on," and walked out followed by fifteen or twenty companions.
At the "cooler" where the prisoner was held, they searched the six guards for the keys and, finding none, broke down the door with an ax from a woodpile.
The leader brought the gambler out with the noose around his neck and the crowd led him to an old building whose beam jutted over the sidewalk.
Asked if he had anything to say, the gambler offered the $1,900 in his pockets if they would shoot him instead, and the leader refused, saying he had murdered a good man.
When he was first pulled up he grasped the rope with his untied hands, so the men let him down, tied his hands and hanged him again, leaving him for nearly an hour.
Once he was dead, the "committee" sent for a photographer and had a picture taken of the group with the body hanging behind them.
The gambler's companion was given six hours to leave town, and the sketch ends with his joke that he was "five hours ahead of time."
No arrests, inquest on the lynched man or other official response are mentioned.
The piece ran as miscellany on page three of the Somerset Press beside a column of children's sayings, under the headline "An Episode of Border Life."

It casts the lynching as frontier color, praising the dead officer as "a thoroughly good officer," calling the gambler "the murderer" and noting that the proceedings were "as quiet as could possibly be."
The narrator closes by calling the hanging his "first initiation into Western life."

accounts.gist: An eyewitness narrator recalls a gambler shooting a police officer, and miners leaving the inquest to break into the cooler and hang him, then photographing themselves with the body.

framing.detail: Headed 'An Episode of Border Life' and closing 'This was my first initiation into Western life', the sketch treats the hanging as frontier color, praising the officer, calling the victim 'the murderer' and stressing that the proceedings were quiet.

record_check.dossier: Accused, in a witness's sworn inquest testimony, of shooting a police officer through the heart over a card quarrel.
'Jim' is how the leader addresses the gambler; the narrator's companion is also called Jim, and Jim Beggs is the saloon keeper, so no surname is known.

info: Not stated; the sketch is a reminiscence of the narrator's 'first initiation into Western life', reprinted 16 June 1881. The killing of the officer took place in the evening and the hanging the next early morning.
An unnamed Western mining town ('border life'); the gambler was held in the 'cooler' and hanged from a beam jutting over the sidewalk from an old building on the street.
A richly dressed gambler addressed as 'Jim'; no surname or race given.
Accused, in sworn testimony before a coroner's jury, of shooting a police officer through the heart during a quarrel over cards in Jim Beggs' gambling saloon.
Miners led by a 'strapping big fellow' in a red flannel shirt; the narrator calls them the 'lynchers', the 'committee' and the 'gang'.
The gambler's companion was given six hours to leave town.

sources.note: Undated, unplaced first-person sketch credited to the Pittsburgh Post: miners take a gambler 'Jim' from the jail 'cooler' during the inquest on a police officer he shot, hang him from a beam and pose for a photograph.
quotes: wake up or you will miss the lynching.

You murdered a good man, and you've got to swing for it.
The entire proceedings were as quiet as could possibly be; not a word or shout could be heard.
This was my first initiation into Western life.
